prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength allow frequency comparison at the 1e-18 level, and for its realisation as a reproducible standard

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my preferred single-part prize, and I want to say precisely why after the first round. The scientific step is a specific physical idea: choose the trapping wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, and the atoms can be held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil effects while thousands of them are interrogated at once. That is not an engineering refinement of the 2005 comb or the 2012 single-ion work; it is a different regime, and it was only confirmed because several laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) reached agreeing uncertainties near 1e-18 and compared them over fibre links. Agreement between independent experiments and the theory of the shifts (blackbody, lattice, collisional) is the kind of evidence I trust most. The two-name credit is clean, and Kroll's and my reading is that the concept and its realisation are what the citation should name, so the earlier prizes are not duplicated. I tried this round to see whether the topological-insulator case should displace it, and I explain below why it has not, while saying plainly that B018 is a strong prize that I would be content to see awarded.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses are three. First, novelty against earlier metrology prizes is a judgement and not a fact; a committee may read the lattice clock as a second-generation advance. Second, fundamental-physics output so far consists of constraints (no drift of constants, no dark-matter signal), so the discovery content is the capability and not a new phenomenon, as Eriksson and Mehlig correctly point out. Third, priority is not fully tidy: I recall the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstration as Katori's and the Tokyo group's, with Ye's group, SYRTE, PTB and NIST driving the accuracy frontier, but I have not been able to check dates against the primary papers and the credit between concept and performance is an interpretive choice. Against my own preference, B018 has six supporters from varied fields, the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is by their account a separable discovery with nearly two decades of independent confirmation, and the condensed-matter members, who know that field far better than I do, find the trio coherent. The remaining gap in the record (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan) is a real cost that I cannot weigh as well as they can.

responses.point: Kroll asked me, as the atomic-structure specialist, to check the magic-wavelength priority dates against his memory and noted that the concept and first neutral-atom lattice clock are Katori's.
responses.response: I can only confirm the broad picture from memory, not the exact dates: the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice-clock demonstration came from Katori's group in Tokyo in the early to mid 2000s, and the proposal was developed in parallel by theorists, which is why I would not let the citation speak of anyone else having first thought of the shift cancellation without a check. The experts should verify this against the primary papers before the ballot. I agree with him that the citation should name the concept and its realisation, and I have worded mine that way. Where I would go slightly further is on the reproduction: the fact that Ye's group, PTB, SYRTE and others later reached the same uncertainty without Katori's apparatus is what lifts this from a good proposal to a robust discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson says the 2D quantum spin Hall effect is the cleaner, separable discovery and that its independent confirmation is at least as extensive as for the clocks, while the fundamental-physics output of clocks is so far constraints.
responses.response: I accept the point about separability and I accept that it is a more clearly new phenomenon: a topologically protected edge state is something nobody had seen. Where I still differ is on two things. The HgTe quantisation is imperfect over longer edges, as he himself notes, whereas the clock numbers have been reproduced to the quoted precision in several laboratories. And the credit is clean for clocks and visibly incomplete for the topological insulators. I do not think my differences should outweigh his judgement of how central the 2D case is; they only say that these are two good candidates differing in kind, one a new phase and one a new way of measuring, and I would not argue strongly against the committee choosing B018 if it settles the citation wording.

responses.point: Olsson says she would not oppose B041 but ranks it behind B018 because the original experiment and the people are clearer for topological insulators, and she worries about parallel contributions and the comb and ion-clock lineage.
responses.response: I do not think the original experiment is clearer for B018 than for the lattice clock; for B018 the chain runs through the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp what to build, and she herself lists that as the decisive concern, whereas for the clock the proposal and the first realisation sit with Katori. On parallel contributions I agree there is a real question, but the competing groups confirmed the idea and drove its performance; they did not conceive a different method. I do agree with her that the lineage must be handled in the citation, and for that reason I describe the invention of the lattice scheme and not frequency metrology generally.

responses.point: Mehlig finds B041 the strongest alternative to B018 but questions what is new in physics terms, since the payoff so far is constraints and the central step is Katori's rather than Ye's performance.
responses.response: This is the question I should answer directly. What is new in physics terms is the combination of an exactly engineered cancellation of a perturbation with a many-atom ensemble, which makes systematic shifts controllable and lets the ensemble average down statistically; the demonstrations of millimetre-scale gravitational redshift in the laboratory and of fibre-link agreement across continents are consequences that nobody could measure before. I agree that Katori's idea and Ye's performance are separate things, and my two-name credit gives each a part: concept and first realisation for Katori, and the demonstration that the scheme reaches 1e-18 with controlled many-body effects for Ye. Whether that is enough is for the committee to judge and I do not claim certainty.

responses.point: Pearce said he under-weighted clocks at opening but now prefers B018, keeping B041 as first alternative, and raised a precision-measurement pairing as a possible two-part prize that the three-person limit makes hard to configure.
responses.response: I am glad he regards the independent validation across laboratories as persuasive. On the two-part idea, I looked at pairing B041 with B018 and it cannot be honoured: five names exceed three, and I do not want to cut Ye or Molenkamp to fit the limit. So the committee has to choose, and I would not stretch a configuration to produce consensus. On his timing point I agree the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to expect a better record soon, but it is not a requirement, since the science stands on its own and the redefinition is a consequence, not the discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges optical lattice clocks distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I regard this as the central judgement and cannot settle it by argument alone.

The exact priority dates of the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstration, and the relative decisiveness of Katori and Ye; I rely on memory and the experts should check the primary papers.
Whether the B018 gap (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan) is acceptable and whether HgTe edge quantisation is sufficient; I defer to the condensed-matter members.
Whether my own subfield proximity (precision atomic physics) leads me to rate clocks higher than members outside it would.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye listed in my record, and no link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the B010 names. My close ties are to Anne L'Huillier and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and to Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato, none of whom are credited here. General membership of the atomic, molecular and optical community is a normal professional connection and not a recusal ground.
